name: calc
why: Landon Curt Noll's arbitrary precision calculator comes with its own C-like language and a long mathematical pedigree that rewards exploration.

brief.what_it_is: Calc is an interactive arbitrary-precision calculator with its own C-style programming language. You type expressions or statements and it prints the results. It can also take a single command as a command-line argument, run it, and exit. Values are kept as fractions with arbitrarily large numerators and denominators, reduced to lowest terms. It supports complex numbers, transcendental functions, and output as fractions, hex, octal, or binary.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the authors wrote calc "because they wanted to write it, because it was fun writing it, and because we wanted you to use and enjoy it." The README frames it as a tool for easy large numeric calculations that can also be programmed for difficult or long calculations.
brief.how_it_works: Each input line is treated as the body of a procedure in a C-like language, so it can hold declarations, expressions, labels, conditionals, and loops. Every non-assignment expression is printed automatically. Functions can be defined with 'define' in C-like syntax or with an '=' shorthand. Variables can be global, local, or static, and are untyped.

brief.install_notes: Packages are listed for yum, pacman, apt (Debian and Ubuntu), dnf, and Termux, and the README also gives a source build with 'sudo make clobber all chk install'. The homepage says official releases are RPMs and source tarballs on GitHub. Environment variables CALCRC, CALCPATH, and CALCHISTFILE configure it, and it falls back to XDG directories when those are unset. The README does not mention brew, though the catalogue entry uses it.
brief.standout: The language is C-like but with its own rules, and the README includes a 'help unexpected' page for C programmers who will be surprised. Its mathematical pedigree is notable: the homepage says the lucas.cal script contains methods used to find a very large prime, and it links a tutorial on finding new largest known primes.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. The homepage's revision line is dated 2022/07/07 and its copyright runs 1994-2013. The GitHub repo has master (stable releases), calcv3 (experimental, described as active work toward 64-bit and larger support), and legacy-calc branches, and it links a security policy, which suggests ongoing upkeep. I did not see a release date or last-commit date.
brief.caveats: Very old systems may fail to build the master branch: it needs a c17 compiler, int64_t and uint64_t, and a boolean type. Those systems should use the legacy-calc branch, frozen at 2.16.1.x. The calcv3 branch is labeled experimental. The homepage licence is the GNU Lesser General Public License version 2.1. The homepage was reachable, but its links to the release, tutorial, and curious-primes pages are given as text with no URLs, so I did not follow them.
quotes: Calc is an interactive calculator which provides for easy large numeric calculations, but which also can be easily programmed for difficult or long calculations.
When in doubt, use the master branch.
